title: Explain Sliding Window: fixed-size vs variable-size window, expand right / shrink left.
shortTitle: Explain Sliding Window: Fixed-Size vs Variable-Size, Expand Right / Shrink Left
keyPoints: Sliding window maintains a contiguous range with two indexes, updating a running result incrementally in O(n)
Fixed-size window slides one step at a time: add the entering element and subtract the leaving element
Variable-size window grows right and shrinks left based on a condition
Longest-valid: shrink while invalid, then record width; shortest-valid: shrink while valid, recording minimum
Amortized O(n) because the left pointer only advances and each element enters and leaves once
Many window problems carry a frequency map or count to check validity in O(1) per step

s1_definition.oneliner: Expand right to add, shrink left to remove, and update the answer incrementally, turning repeated subrange scans into one linear pass.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Sliding window** – a technique that maintains a contiguous range over an array or string using two indexes, updating a running result in O(n) instead of recomputing over every subrange.
- **Fixed-size window** – keeps a constant width K and slides one step at a time, adding the entering element and subtracting the leaving element.
- **Variable-size window** – grows the right edge in an outer loop and shrinks the left edge in an inner loop based on a condition.
- **Amortized linear** – even with the nested inner loop, each element enters and leaves the window exactly once, giving O(n) total work.
- **Validity tracking** – many problems use a frequency map or a counter to check window validity in O(1) per step.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh at the National Bank of India watches a rolling window of recent transactions. For a fixed window he always looks at exactly the last K transactions, dropping the oldest as a new one arrives. For a variable window he keeps extending as long as the running total stays within a limit and pulls the left edge in when it crosses the limit, so the window breathes in and out.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The sliding window technique keeps a contiguous range over an array or string using two indexes, expanding the right edge to bring new elements in and contracting the left edge to drop old ones, while updating a running result incrementally. This turns problems that recompute an aggregate over every subrange into a single linear pass.

There are two flavors. A fixed-size window has a width given by the problem. You build the initial window over the first K elements, then slide one step at a time by adding the entering element and subtracting the leaving element, keeping the aggregate current in O(1) per step. A variable-size window grows and shrinks based on a condition: for a longest-valid problem you shrink while the window is invalid, and for a shortest-valid problem you shrink while the window is still valid.

The amortized linear time is what makes the technique powerful. Even with the nested inner loop, the left pointer only moves forward, so each element enters and leaves the window exactly once. The total work across the entire outer loop is O(n), not O(n^2).

In the fraud engine at the National Bank of India, Rajesh uses both variants. A fixed three-transaction rolling sum flags sudden spending bursts. A variable window finds the longest recent streak of transactions whose total stays within a daily safe limit. Recognizing whether a problem needs fixed or variable, and whether the shrink direction is longest or shortest, is the key to applying the technique correctly.

Remember one sentence: expand right to include, shrink left to exclude, update the answer incrementally, and the amortized cost stays linear.
